title: The Last Eagle – a 5-minute look at my solo medieval RPG (Work in Progress)
author: DometGames
selftext:
Hi everyone! Some of you might remember my previous post – here's a 5-minute teaser stitched together from different parts of the game: the world map, towns, villages, taverns, the market, character creation and the arena.



I'm a solo developer working in Godot, and AI is a big part of how one person can build something this size. Most props and the UI art started as AI-generated 3D models and images, which I then clean up, retexture and fit into the game. On the code side I work with an AI coding assistant for gameplay systems, tools and pipeline scripts – things like batch-processing models in Blender, checking geometry, and building the capture and editing tools that made this very video. Characters, animations and the building kits are purchased packs that I adapt and extend.  


There's a lot more I'd like to show, but I'm not happy with how some parts look yet. Right now I'm trying to raise enough to fix the things that bother me most.



Everything shown is a work in progress.

comments.author: Austin_Ox23
comments.body: a pretty ambitious project a solo developer, what's been the biggest challenge so far, getting all the different systems together or rebuilding the world itself?

replies.author: DometGames
replies.body:
Thanks! Honestly, getting everything to work together has been the hardest part. Each system on its own is manageable – the world map, towns, villages, characters, animations – but once they all have to live in one game, things start breaking in unexpected places. Performance in the towns was a big one, with lots of people, grass and buildings on screen at once.

The other big challenge is making everything look like it belongs to the same world. Assets come from different sources, so getting the scale, materials and lighting consistent takes much more time than you'd expect.

comments.author: FlykeSpice
comments.body:
Do you clean up the topology from the 3d generated models as well? I'm not familiar with them but from what I see samples on sketchfab they have horrible topology that can easily kill perfomance on basic games (besides messed up textures).

How about overall perfomance from the code? if there is one thing that most AI generated games fail in this sub is their games have suboptimal perfomance for seemingly basic scenes.

replies.author: DometGames
replies.body:
Good question! Yes – raw generated models are usually way too heavy and messy. I reduce the polycount, fix or rebake the textures, lower texture resolutions where they don't need to be high, and add LODs so distant objects are much cheaper. Small props get batched together when there are many of them on screen.

Performance from the code is something I measure constantly, and I don't trust the AI's code without checking it in the profiler. The towns were the hardest part – lots of people, grass and buildings at once. For example, I got grass rendering down from about 6.8 ms to 3.8 ms per frame, and characters far from the camera update their animations less often. It's still not where I want it in the busiest towns, so that's one of the things I'm working on right now.

replies.author: FlykeSpice
replies.body:
Yes, profiling your code is the best way to yield bigger perfomance gains because they actually point to the biggest hot spots in your code that you need to focus optimizing on.

I'm curious about your choice of Godot, is it because you were already familiar with it before or you thought it could work best with AI? 

From what I have heard it's pretty rough on edges with open-world games.

comments.author: dilberry
comments.body: Looks fantastic - this is a huge undertaking for one person. I think most people have no idea how hard it is to get a game looking/playing like this by yourself.

replies.author: DometGames
replies.body: Thank you so much, that really means a lot!
